body:
@flocsy - Leg vs sub-journey vs journey: The understanding is that a sub-journey is contiguous, and not just any subset. This is indicated in the definition that the legs must be "connected by transfers", but I will add the word "contiguous" to make this more clear. - "Prefix": Good catch, that was certainly not a valid definition of a "sub-journey". - Your extended fares model: Do you have documentation published somewhere that we can reference? I'm interested in seeing this in detail.
### Fare transfer processing I took up the exercise of defining `fare_transfer_type` processing and interactions to get more precise about how they should be used and have a clear consensus on this. Taking the current definitions, this is how a 2-leg transfer would be processed (variables represent the cost of the leg or transfer): ![2-leg transfer](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62957380/144116057-d5cf7ef0-1a67-4e65-922c-10140e410459.png) | `fare_transfer_type` | Processing A > B | | ----- | ----- | | `0` | A + AB | | `1` | A + AB + B | | `2` | MAX(A, B) + AB | | `3` | AB |
Now where things get interesting, 3-leg transfer interactions: ![3-leg-transfer](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62957380/144116095-8a0aedae-5235-4782-a58f-e0b3644dd5f2.png) Piecewise processing: - `[]>` and `>[]` indicates that the incoming transfer process result can be "plugged" into an outgoing transfer process. - `+` indicates that the outgoing transfer process result is added to the incoming transfer process result. | `fare_transfer_type` | Processing A > B | Processing B > C | | ----- | ----- | ----- | | `0` | [A + AB]> | >[B] + BC | | `1` | [A + AB + B]> | >[B] + BC + C | | `2` | [MAX(A, B) + AB]> | + MAX(B, C) + BC | | `3` | [AB]> | + BC | Looking at how these would interact in different arrangements, I think all the cases are straightforward, except for 2>2. I see two reasonable options, delimited by "?or" in the table below. 1. Process each leg pair separately, and then choose the max (leg+transfer) price. 2. Process each leg pair piecewise and add them together. I think both of these behaviours are equally theoretical to how an agency might structure their fare policy, and as I've mentioned before, chaining `fare_transfer_type=2` seems to be also be an unlikely scenario by a data producer. At any rate, I prefer option 2 as it is more intuitive with the "plug" rules defined in the table above. Meanwhile, option 1 is a fairly arbitrary abstraction on the rules governing a 2-leg transfer (abstracting the same logic to a 3-leg transfer). | B > C
A > B | `0` | `1` | `2` | `3` | | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | | `0` | A + AB + BC | A + AB + BC + C | A + AB + MAX(B, C) + BC | A + AB + BC | | `1` | A + AB + B + BC | A + AB + B + BC + C | A + AB + B + MAX(B, C) + BC | A + AB + B + BC | | `2` | MAX(A, B) + AB + BC | MAX(A, B) + AB + BC + C | MAX((MAX(A, B) + AB), (MAX(B, C) + BC))

?or

MAX(A, B) + AB + MAX(B, C) + BC | MAX(A, B) + AB + BC | | `3` | AB + BC | AB + BC + C | AB + MAX (B, C) + BC | AB + BC | \*Sub-journey A>B is on the row header
\*Sub-journey B>C is on the column header Thoughts on these defined rules and `fare_transfer_type=2`?

I like your tables, and maybe it would be a good idea to add them to the spec (once we agree here on how they should be)

As for the notations, where you plug in the results of previous legs/transfers but you still use [B] on the right side, I think it would be clearer if instead of [B] it would be something like S (for Sum). ie:
0	[A + AB]	S + BC
and because of this I would also change the textual description to describe the steps this way, so that it'll be cleares when you look at both the text and the tables.

body:
> Shouldn't this rather be: "the cost of a sub-journey IS the cost in fare_transfer_rules.amount"? 

This is a cleaner description (I like it) but it doesn't capture what happens when we "chain" multiple legs in a journey (i.e., the interaction of `fare_transfer_type` illustrated [here](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#discussion_r759636579)).

I'm wondering if in light of the brainstorming on `fare_transfer_type` interactions, we should drop the concept of "sub-journey" all-together in these descriptions. As you have pointed out, it's not clear what a sub-journey is, and the fact that it can actually be any contiguous subset of a journey is not actually helpful when describing `fare_transfer_type` interactions and their chaining.

Here is my proposal to clean up the description of `fare_transfer_type`:

> Indicates the cost processing method of transferring between legs in a journey:
> 
> ![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62957380/144116057-d5cf7ef0-1a67-4e65-922c-10140e410459.png) 
> Valid options are:
> `0` - `fare_leg_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_transfer_rules.amount`; A + AB.
> `1` - `fare_leg_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_transfer_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_leg_rules.amount` for the transferred leg; A + AB + B.
> `2` - The leg with the most expensive `fare_leg_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_transfer_rules.amount` ; MAX(A, B) + AB.
> `3` - `fare_transfer_rules.amount`; AB.
> 
> Cost processing interactions of transferring between legs in a journey with more than 2 legs:
>
> ![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62957380/144116095-8a0aedae-5235-4782-a58f-e0b3644dd5f2.png)
> | `fare_transfer_type` | Processing A > B | Processing B > C |
> | ----- | ----- | ----- | 
> | `0` | A + AB | S + BC |
> | `1` | A + AB + B | S + BC + C |
> | `2` | MAX(A, B) + AB | S + MAX(B, C) + BC |
> | `3` | AB | S + BC |
> 
> Where S indicates the total calculated cost of the preceding leg(s) and transfer(s).

Does this clarify all possible uses?

The case you described would likely be covered using the `duration_limit` fields in `fare_transfer_rules.txt`. I.e., unlimited transfers within X minutes.

For more complex transfer sequence rules, see `fare_transfer_rules.txt` fields `transfer_id` and `transfer_sequence`, as well as example S in the working doc: http://bit.ly/gtfs-fares. 

Since that feature is out of scope for this PR, please voice any feedback on that model in the doc!

body:
I don't really understand your last comment. It sounds like we're talking about a B2B contract where the 2 sides agree which format the provider produces. But this is not the case IMHO. Producers automatically generate and publish the GTFS, and consumers consume it. The producer probably doesn't even know most of the consumers. Think about the countless apps. I thought the whole point of GTFS and especially the huge effort mobilitydata invests in these changes is to have more and more publicly available and up-to-date, and precise data.

I agree that if an agency that doesn't have today fares in GTFS starts to produce it after this change passes it makes sense to only provide V2 (aka: it might be not very useful immediately because only a few consumers will be ready to read it, but it doesn't create a regression, because it doesn't exist today, so nobody uses V1). But it's a different situation when an agency has a publicly available GTFS with fares V1 in it. If they would stop producing the V1 a month after the vote passes it would suddenly render this agency's fares non-existant for many consumers. And because there is no B2B relationship we can't even say things like "let's have a 3 month period when we still provide V1 but already provide V2 to give the consumer time to adapt"...

> > Shouldn't this rather be: "the cost of a sub-journey IS the cost in fare_transfer_rules.amount"?
> 
> This is a cleaner description (I like it) but it doesn't capture what happens when we "chain" multiple legs in a journey (i.e., the interaction of `fare_transfer_type` illustrated [here](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/286#discussion_r759636579)).

Still the 1st part of the sentence is confusing IMHO. What about something different: "The cost of the sub-journey is [only?] the cost of fare_transfer_rules.amount which overrides the costs from the previous legs and transfers"?

> 
> I'm wondering if in light of the brainstorming on `fare_transfer_type` interactions, we should drop the concept of "sub-journey" all-together in these descriptions. As you have pointed out, it's not clear what a sub-journey is, and the fact that it can actually be any contiguous subset of a journey is not actually helpful when describing `fare_transfer_type` interactions and their chaining.
> 
> Here is my proposal to clean up the description of `fare_transfer_type`:
> 
> > Indicates the cost processing method of transferring between legs in a journey:
> > ![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62957380/144116057-d5cf7ef0-1a67-4e65-922c-10140e410459.png)
> > Valid options are:
> > `0` - `fare_leg_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_transfer_rules.amount`; A + AB.
> > `1` - `fare_leg_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_transfer_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_leg_rules.amount` for the transferred leg; A + AB + B.
> > `2` - The leg with the most expensive `fare_leg_rules.amount` plus the cost of `fare_transfer_rules.amount` ; MAX(A, B) + AB.
> > `3` - `fare_transfer_rules.amount`; AB.
> > Cost processing interactions of transferring between legs in a journey with more than 2 legs:
> > ![](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/62957380/144116095-8a0aedae-5235-4782-a58f-e0b3644dd5f2.png)
> > 
> > 
> > 
> > `fare_transfer_type`
> > Processing A > B
> > Processing B > C
> > 
> > 
> > 
> > 
> > `0`
> > A + AB
> > S + BC
> > 
> > 
> > `1`
> > A + AB + B
> > S + BC + C
> > 
> > 
> > `2`
> > MAX(A, B) + AB
> > S + MAX(B, C) + BC
> > 

I think this contradicts the meaning of the sentence and should instead be: MAX(A, ..., C) + BC (or something similar, the main point is that "S+" shouldn't be there) but it also shows that there is some kind of problem with this rule (even now, without mentioning "sub-journeys"). For example it's easy to imagine the following situation: on buses you pay per distance or whatever way, on subway legs you only pay for the longest (most expensive) leg. The problem is that when you mix them i.e: Subway1, Bus2, Subway3, Bus4 and the cost would be: max(S1,S3) + B2 + B4, then this notation won't work.

> > 
> > `3`
> > AB
> > S + BC
> > 
> > 
> > 
> > Where S indicates the total calculated cost of the preceding leg(s) and transfer(s).
> 
> Does this clarify all possible uses?

I think we should still think about the non-consecutive cases. In the table for the "more than 2 legs" journeys it is even now implicitly required to have consecutive legs (because of A, B. C and S). I think there should be a way to easily understand from the spec that cases like the above example with the buses and subways having different fare system so the total cost of the full journey will be the sum of the "sub-journeys" (buses + subways) are possible and legal. But of course there could be many more examples (different agencies have different fare system, so the "sub-journeys" in this case would be agency_set1 + agency_set2 + ...)

body:
I think this is overthinking the transition. The transition will happen naturally and I don't think the spec should dictate the best way to do it. 

Consumers should be aware of the transition. If they are not, I think it's their responsibility to be. Producers will not drop fares v1 data until a good amount of consumers will support it. If they do, it will be a conscious choice in doing so.

body: Can you squash all your commits? It is pretty hard to follow what is actually changed? And if the table is just moved to another place and reformatted put it in a separate commit, please.

I agree, it is. The reason for the change is that it hasn't been clear to newcomers in the spec, especially those that aren't familiar with the rules of protobufs, what the default value is here. Also, we should change this to be consistent, as StopTimeUpdate.schedule_relationship already has an explicit default defined in the .proto:

https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs-realtime/proto/gtfs-realtime.proto#L252-L253

```proto
    optional ScheduleRelationship schedule_relationship = 5
        [default = SCHEDULED];
```

>The UNSCHEDULED has a comment mentioning that it is experimental and subject to change.

So there are two different schedule_relationship.UNSCHEDULED enumerations:
1. [`TripDescriptor.schedule_relationship.UNSCHEDULED`](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs-realtime/proto/gtfs-realtime.proto#L794-L796) - This field is NOT experimental. This change is related to this field.
2. [`StopTimeUpdate.schedule_relationship.UNSCHEDULED`](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs-realtime/proto/gtfs-realtime.proto#L252-L253) - This field is experimental, but only because we haven't seen anyone publish it in the wild. Conceptually it exists for the exact same reason as `TripDescriptor.schedule_relationship.UNSCHEDULED`.

>This will cause us to lose realtime for all frequency based trips, as we currently don't handle UNSCHEDULED. 

From your response it sounds like there are producers labeling updates for exact_times=0 trips with `schedule_relationship.SCHEDULED` - is that right? If so I'd argue that already goes against the spec - it's pretty clear from the existing spec that those updates should be labeled with UNSCHEDULED. 

That being said, this is the problem we're trying to solve with this PR, so if there are widespread issues with existing producers doing this wrong then we might need a migration path forward to get everyone in-line with the spec. Thoughts on this are welcome.
May be 'scheduled start time'? The 'initially scheduled' implies that it can be another scheduled time.

"Trips with ScheduleRelationship=UNSCHEDULED must also set all 
 stopTimeUpdates.ScheduleRelationship=UNSCHEDULED"
It looks non-experimental field suggests to use experimental feed? It is very confusing. Agency setting STU.schedule_relationship = UNSCHEDULED will be surprised that their updates are dropped because we actually don't support this experimental value and require STU.SCHEDULED for such STUs. There is actually a schedule for stop times even for exact_times=0. It just happen that the start of the schedule is shifted to the trip 'start_time' of the trip. I believe agency can express relationship to the schedule in terms of STU.{arrival,departure}.delay. That schedule will also be used if agency haven't specified any STU for a stop and the stop arrival/departure times will be deduced from it.

I'm intentionally trying not to use the word "scheduled" here because the `TripDescriptor` can refer to both scheduled (normal GTFS without frequencies.txt, frequencies.txt exact_times=1) and frequency-based (frequencies.txt exact_times=0) trips. I'm currently proposing that we change the text to just:

>The start time of this trip instance.

...and let the remainder of the paragraph describe the conditions under which it's scheduled or frequency-based.

IMHO it's already confusing enough that we have scheduled trips represented in frequencies.txt with exact_times=1 trips, so I'd like to be more precise in the language and not use "schedule" when referring to exact_times=0 trips.

>Agency setting STU.schedule_relationship = UNSCHEDULED will be surprised that their updates are dropped because we actually don't support this experimental value and require STU.SCHEDULED for such STUs. 

@IvanVolosyuk How about we put some language here to make it clearer that consumers may choose to continue to process this type of data while producers transition to what the spec says? Some like what's in [TripDescriptor](https://github.com/google/transit/blob/master/gtfs-realtime/spec/en/reference.md#message-tripdescriptor):

"If any enumeration other than UNSCHEDULED is used for exact_times=0 trips it is considered an error and the entity containing the erroneous TripDescriptor may be discarded by consumers."

The "may" here allows you to continue consuming this if you want, even if it doesn't adhere to the spec.

>There is actually a schedule for stop times even for exact_times=0. It just happen that the start of the schedule is shifted to the trip 'start_time' of the trip. I believe agency can express relationship to the schedule in terms of STU.{arrival,departure}.delay. That schedule will also be used if agency haven't specified any STU for a stop and the stop arrival/departure times will be deduced from it.

tl;dr - I've opened an issue [here](https://github.com/google/transit/issues/314) to discuss this specifically - please comment!

For this PR I'd like to stick to clarifying the existing text without getting into those details.

Regarding other cases: this is tricky, because it really can depend on whatever the operator decides. I can imagine for example that one operator decides that the fares are decided by the schedule (even if there's a delay and the bus leaves at 09:03 instead of the scheduled 08:57 and even though from 09:00 it would be peek time you still pay as it was off-time) but another operator decides that what matters is the time the bus leaves the stop (or maybe rather the time you touch your card)

The point is that even though we might not be able to use the different cases to calculate the fare in advance, but even then having the information in the GTFS is useful because it can be displayed to the user.

This again is really impossible in DB, which means it could only be implemented by not using foreign keys and do something else that is more complicated if even possible. I think it should be clear from the data what it is meant. Using the prefixes as I suggested in area_id is better, but even that doesn't really solve the problem that one field should be foreign key to different tables. body:
We've managed to keep these values distinct at the DB level with no issue. Our `area_id`s are generated in the same table as our `stop_id`s in ascending order, so there's no risk of overlap there, and we do use a prefix for location `id`s.

Using a prefix to ensure these values don't overlap is good advice, but I do not think it needs to be a requirement of the spec.

Logically, I guess I don't see the validation hurdle: "Does this id appear in stops.txt? Does this id appear in locations.geojson? Does this id appear in areas.txt? If no to all, passes validation" seems fairly straightforward.

Yes, good catch, it should be added. @tzujenchanmbd 

> It is NOT a stop_id, so let's not call it that. Maybe geographical_reference or stop_location?

The original iteration of Flex (v1) had a separate field in stop_times to refer only to polygons, but you still had to define `stop_times.stop_id` since it is a required field. Because of this, you had to use a "dummy" id in `stop_times.stop_id` which, the v2 drafting community decided, was worse than just having `stop_times.stop_id` able to reference ids from multiple files.

body:
As a consumer (OBA, OTP) I've also had no issue with these IDs sharing a global ID space. Yes, it does make validation and lookup a bit more complicated but considering all the other complexities of the Flex spec, this is the easy part.

It's probably a good idea to prefix your IDs but that should really be left to the producer. I would not want to add any kind of ID requirements to the spec. IMO GTFS should treat them as transparent identifiers with no meta data encoded into them, which it currently does.

body:
I accept Gavriel's point about this being a little difficult to model in a relational database but I don't believe that it must be the goal of the spec to make it so.

I also agree that using the name "stop_location" (which we do in our internal model) would have been preferable if this was part of the first iteration of GTFS ~15 years ago.

However, given that GTFS has no versions and pretty ironclad backwards-compatibility guarantees, I think using stop_id rather than introducing a new field is the least bad solution given the constraints that we face. For my part, I have been consuming the stop_id that refers to three different types of entities for years and it has not given me any issues that are worse than all the other problems that exist when you mix static and flexible transit data.

Having said that, I would be open to do a consensus finding exercise to figure out what the community thinks.

Lastly, I would like to emphasize that I don't want to dismiss Gavriel's points but rather argue that GTFS is in many ways highly pragmatic which _does_ lead these kinds of design decisions. On balance, I think I'm happier with this approach compared to what other standards follow which say that they follow more "robust" engineering principles.

The stop or station of the fare leg’s departure event should be used for timezone resolution, where appropriate.

For a fare leg rule that specifies a `from_timeframe_group_id`, that rule will match a particular leg if either `from_timeframe_group_id` is empty, or if there exists at least one row in `timeframes.txt` where all of the following conditions are true
- The row’s `timeframe_group_id` is equal to the `from_timeframe_group_id` value.
- The set of days identified by the row’s `service_id` contains the “current day” of the fare leg’s start time.
- The fare leg’s “time-of-day” is greater than or equal to the row’s `start_time` value and less than the `end_time` value.

body: Given that there is a phone number field that exists elsewhere in the core spec, defining a best practice for number format should be discussed outside of this PR (but this PR shouldn't be contingent on that discussion since it would be a question of general best practice/"recommended" for a certain field type as opposed to specific field requirements).

Most consumers do have an internal model of a stop pattern but is that actually part of the spec? It feels a huge opportunity to generate lots of invalid updates by refering to a concept that isn't defined anywhere.

(I do see that otherwise you'd have to generate a lot of duplicates.)

I would like this to be mandatory. 

I understand that in the situations were talking about here the agencies often don't truly know at what times the bus will be at the stop but in most systems (OTP included) each stop time must have a, well, time, otherwise the routing algorithm doesn't work. 

So in the absence of this data it would have to be guessed/interpolated somewhere and I would prefer there to be only one place where these interpolations happen, namely in the system that is producing the realtime update, rather than separate guesses in OTP, Google Maps, Transit ...

I recognize that this is a little against the spirit of the `TripUpdate` which allows you to leave out a lot of stuff but this creates a lot of ambiguity and makes applying updates harder than necessary.
These drawings are very illustrative - well done!

+# Trip Modifications
+
+A `TripModifications` message identifies a list of similar `trip_ids` from the (CSV) GTFS sharing the same stop pattern, which are all affected by a particular modification, such as a detour.
+
+## SLO: Service-level objective
+
+The frequency of data updates is expected to be approximately hourly (~24 times/day). Ingestion time may depend on the total number of affected trips. Consumers are expected to ingest a single TripModification within 5 minutes, and a feed with hundreds of detours within 20 minutes.
+
+## TripModifications
+
+The modification is in effect on all of the listed service\_dates, until it is removed from the feed. On any given service date, a trip MUST NOT be assigned to more than one `TripModifications` object.
+
+There MAY be multiple `TripModifications` for a given stop pattern. It may be desirable to split the trips into multiple modifications e.g. if the `propagated_modification_delay` changes significantly, over the course of the detour.
+
+The trips created through GTFS-TripModifications modify and replace each specified `trip_id`, and don't create a copy or additional run.
+
+The scheduled stop times of each replacement trip are created from those of the affected trip, by performing the changes listed in modifications. Stop sequences are assigned from 1 to n, increasing by 1 for each stop in the trip. A `TripUpdate` message must be provided to publish real-time arrival/departure times for the replacement trip.
+
+
+## Linkage to TripUpdates
+
+* A TripUpdate SHOULD be provided using the replacement trip ID (`modifications_id` + `_` + `trip_id`). The TripUpdate MAY provide an ETA at the replacement stops.
+* If no such TripUpdate is found, TripUpdates for the original `trip_id` will apply to the modified trip. In this case, no ETA is available at the replacement stops.
+
+##  Modification
+
+A `Modification` message replaces a span of n stop times (`num_stops_replaced`) from each affected trip starting at `start_stop_sequence`. The spans of the modifications MUST not overlap. Spans may not be contiguous; in this case the two modifications MUST be merged into one.  These stop times are replaced with a new stop time for each replacement stop described by `replacement_stops`.
+
+The sequence of `replacement_stops` may be of arbitrary length. For example, 3 stops could be replaced by 2, 4, or 0 stops as the situation may require.

These stop times are replaced with a new stop time for each replacement stop described by `replacement_stops`.

We're not changing anything on the spec in regard on how feeds can contain multiple types of entities or not : ["A feed may, although not required to, combine entities of different types."](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/403/files#diff-90f282d10f519d763309d02a8161020994bcf89cfc6d45dabc6376e2b0c5492dR22) Swiftly merges TripModif with TripUpdates but we support any configuration. This section is to "manage expectations" that consumer can't ingest that type of data in seconds like we do for all other types of RT feeds. It's inspired by [Service-Changes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1oPfQ6Xvui0g3xiy1pNiyu5cWFLhvrTVyvYsMVKGyGWM/edit#heading=h.dk9syw20pc6j), but I'm not sure how required it is.

I had a question about the linkage to TripUpdates.  I recognize there has been some back-and-forth on this in the comments, based on feedback from IBI Group and others, and I'm reflecting on the behavior of what happens for consumers who haven't updated yet to support trip modifications.

Apologies if I missed this up-thread, but I'm guessing you considered (and discarded) the option to just supply a TripUpdate with the existing `trip_id` that includes updates for:
* existing stops (no real change here)
* new stops in the trip (with possibly a new StopTimeUpdate. ScheduleRelationship enum value)
* skipped stops (either not mentioned at all or explicitly marking them SKIPPED)

When I think about consumers who might be slow to support trip modifications directly, having the separate trip update with a modified trip id would require some level of modification processing.  On the other hand, if the trip id was the same, these consumers might be able to more gracefully fallback to still apply stop time updates to their existing concept of the trip and hide the skipped stops (assuming they support SKIPPED).

I recognize `StopTimeUpdate.stop_sequence` indexing gets a bit murky here.

I'm not necessarily sure this is a good idea, but since you are using `TranslatedString` here (aka using GTFS-RT modeling concepts), would it make sense to use `Position` for the stop location as well?  I know that comes with additional fields that don't necessarily make sense for a stop and maybe that's enough to reject the idea, but I felt compelled to ask.
I'm a neutral on this, I do see a small benefit and small chance of confusion if we do this

To be clear, I think I'm mostly fine with the high-level concept of a first-class "Trip Modification" itself (aka I'm not proposing to cram all this behavior into TripUpdates only).  But I'm keen to understand what TripUpdates would look like in a feed with modifications.

Swiftly has already mentioned that they are going down the path of publishing separate GTFS-Realtime feeds based on whether a consumer can handle trip modifications or not.  I know that's not the first instance of this happening with GTFS data in general, but it's still not a great precedent to set.  I'd rather just have one feed where a consumer who doesn't support TripModifications fully could still get some value out of the feed.  For example, we've already discussed why some consumers might not be able to support detours more generally, but most can realistically handle the skipped stops and stop-time updates for stops that haven't changed along the route.

But maybe this is all just hand-waving around my specific concern: I don't really like the "new trip id" = `modifications_id` + `_` + `trip_id` convention.  I'd rather put `modification_id` as a first-class field in `TripDescriptor` if you need that linkage.  But why is this modification id needed here at all?  If a TripUpdate specifies a trip id for a trip that has an active modification, then that linkage is already specified by the TripModification itself, yes?  Is there are world where a feed would include a TripUpdate for the non-modified trip and for the modified trip as the same time?

I'd say these don't "indicate" groups, but rather these *are* groups of stops:
```suggestion
Defines location groups, which are groups of stops where a rider may request pickup or drop off.
```

However, given that these appear to be only groups of stops, rather than groups of locations (as defined in the other file/table), the name could be confusing. Would it be more consistent and easier to follow if these were called stop_groups or flex_stop_groups instead of location_groups?

It might also be useful to add "in flex services" to the end of this definition, if flex service description is meant to be treated as an optional extension of GTFS and use of this file is considered part of that optional extension.

body: Wording here could be confusing. This says the location_group_id must be unique "across all values" in three files, but then says multiple records in this file (rows in this table) may have the same location_group_id. To create a useful group, of course multiple rows in this table must reference the same location_group_id, which can be seen as the key for an implicit location_group entity that is not materialized in a table. The primary keys of those implicit location_groups then share a namespace with the primary keys of two other tables. The situation is unusual enough that wording will be important to avoid confusing people with more conventional data modeling expectations.

body:
Alternatively, the implicit location_group entities could be materialized in a table. I believe this has been suggested elsewhere, specifically by materializing them as rows in the stops table. Some questions were raised about why it would be useful to do so. By being more consistent with common practices and concepts in data modeling, it allows readers of the spec and consumers of the data to more readily grasp the relationships and constraints present. Approaching this version of the Flex data spec for the first time, it is easier for me to understand that all entities with unique keys from the same namespace appear in one table, and other tables reference those entities via a foreign key to define stop groups or augment them with attributes (such as geometries) that do not fit into fields in the stops table. I'm not necessarily advocating for this approach, just describing why it could be considered beneficial.

Aside: Thinking of one unified table does draw attention to the fact that it's possible to construct recursive stop groups (groups that contain themselves) because via their keys, stop groups are treated as "higher-order stops". This implies something is a bit off with the model here. If all kinds of flex stops have IDs that share a namespace, so could conceivably all appear in the same table, clearly describing which ID can appear where might mean formally factoring out a flex_stops type, which can be visited by flex trips, and is the union of stops, stop_groups, and zones, while stop_groups can only reference stops. The concern here is not about "purity" of a model, but that by doing things that are not fully specified or deviate from convention, the tools in use (such as databases) are less able to help validate data integrity and avoid crash-inducing situations when consuming the data.

Wording here could also be confusing. The definition feels a bit circular: "Locations... defines... locations that indicate groups." Including more of the sentence, this can be condensed to "Locations defines groups... defining zones", which can be further condensed to "Locations define zones".  Is it then fair to say that these locations are just zones? I realize terms stick around for historical reasons, but at this point in the evolution of the spec, would it make more sense to just call these "zones" or "flex_zones"? 

I think there's also the consistency issue I mentioned in another comment, where currently location_groups are not in fact groups of locations. 

Do "groups of lat/lon coordiantes" refer to the interior of the polygons, or to the points defining the perimeter of the polygon? In either case these seem to be details of how the zones are represented or defined, and not the nature of the entities themselves. I believe they're just zone polygons.


Adding something probably relevant here, would love to hear other folks' thoughts.

In our last working group meeting, it was decided to move the table defining stop groups from being shared with fares v2 in `stop_areas.txt` back to using a dedicated file `location_groups.txt`. However, their mechanisms differ:

`stop_areas.txt` has a companion, `areas.txt`. `stop_areas` only assign stops to areas, and multiple entries in `stop_areas` can have the same `area_id`, without including any attributes. The `area_id` in `areas.txt` is a unique ID, and areas.txt contains attributes like `area_name`. When other tables reference the `area_id`, they reference `areas.area_id` rather than `stop_areas.area_id`.

However, the current `location_groups.txt` combines both "grouping" and "indicating attributes" within a single table.

What if we introduce a file similar to `areas.txt` for `location_groups.txt`? This could:
- Ensure a mechanism similar to existing `stop_areas`- `areas` and `route_networks` - `networks` in GTFS (even though they serve different purposes).
- Avoid duplicating values for attributes (such as location_group_name) within a single `location_groups` file.
- **Perhaps alleviate concerns raised in [this comment](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/388#discussion_r1416728745)? (Because the IDs in the new file would be unique ID.)**

body:
> Wording here could be confusing. This says the location_group_id must be unique "across all values" in three files, but then says multiple records in this file (rows in this table) may have the same location_group_id. To create a useful group, of course multiple rows in this table must reference the same location_group_id, which can be seen as the key for an implicit location_group entity that is not materialized in a table. The primary keys of those implicit location_groups then share a namespace with the primary keys of two other tables. The situation is unusual enough that wording will be important to avoid confusing people with more conventional data modeling expectations.

This wording was recently changed to be clearer than it was before. Suggestions to further improve the wording would definitely be welcome! The main point is we want to communicate here is that `stop_id`s, location.geojson `id`s, and `location_group_id`s cannot share the same value (e.g., a `stop_id` and location `id` cannot both equal `abc123`). In the case of `location_group_id`, multiple instances of a given `location_group_id` in location_groups.txt indicate that both those records are within a single location_group.

Regarding the rest:

From a producer perspective, it is more laborious to have to maintain single location groups using **two** files. I'll have to take your word that this feature deviates from conventional structuring of data, but Flex as a spec itself deviates from convention, to use @leonardehrenfried's words, these considerations are the easy part of implementing Flex. We really could spend an endless amount of time iterating components of the spec like this, but at the end of the day, consumers will still need to contend with the bigger challenge of implementing flexible routing. But I still wonder if the two file approach is less complex for a consumer and if mitigating that complexity outweighs the increased complexity for producers? To my knowledge, no Flex consumer since Flex v2's publication over three years ago has ever raised this as an inherent issue of location groups. Yes, areas/stop_areas.txt was momentarily used instead, but for the sole reason of reducing redundancy of file functionality, not because it used two files.

The above comment https://github.com/google/transit/pull/388#discussion_r1417750416 also applies here: the term "flex" doesn't seem to be used in the spec, so some other expression like "on-demand" might be used. 

However, "flex" is clearly a distinct idea in the minds of people drafting the spec, which seems to be intended as a single coherent extension to the spec, and introduces new entities that are specific to this extension and this kind of transportation. It introduces elements that many people will never use, and other people will need to focus on as a specific domain in data pipelines or routing. Both groups need to be able to mentally categorize the growing number of entity types, understand readily which tables "go together" and which ones they need to examine or ignore depending on their use case. To meet those needs, it seems reasonable to qualify the names of new entities with the extension or specific kind of transportation they relate to. This could be done with a prefix, preferably a short memorable one that matches the term used in the proposal or other documents. `flex_` seems like a pretty good candidate to me.

My main point here though was that these may only called "locations" for historical reasons, and it may have long-term benefit to settle on names that better reflect the current role of the entities before the extension is formally adopted. Chains of definitions were built up to say that "locations" are actually geographic polygons that people call "zones" in this kind of transit. In that case, is there any reason they aren't just called "zones"? And if "zones" might be too general because there are also things like "fare zones", then aren't these just on-demand zones or "flex_zones"? That's a nice, short name that says exactly what the table contains and clearly groups it with other tables and concepts only used in on-demand or flex routing, and with proposals and documents pertaining to on-demand or flex routing.

> I agree with @abyrd's wording change suggestion with @tzujenchanmbd's adjustment of "in on-demand service." 

Just to clarify - I did not mean to insist on a specific term ("flex"). The most important point is giving a clear concise signal of context (where and how the entity is used), so readers can mentally filter and group entities and constraints for the particular subset of GTFS extensions they are using, or just better understand the specification. The growing number of entities and relationships can be mentally grouped into coherent chunks associated with documented extensions. This is related to the idea of "gtfs-components" (https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iqvzJV_YWmFyYGtpbO2dqGMbf4XEjvar3rt9SxHU-xY/edit#gid=73504302). Has the idea of gtfs-components been advancing?

>"location_group" was the original name because one could include geojson locations as well as stops.

I think it's important to take a step back and determine whether the terms being used are chosen to be useful to the thousands of people who will need to read and understand this specification and the resulting data, probably for decades to come, or rather they are just familiar to the people who drafted the spec for historical reasons, and conveniently already present in a few prototypes of its use.

> 1. The word "location" has broader application which is convenient if there is potential to add other "location" types to the file if a use case is discovered.

The table is currently structured as a 1-to-N relation between groups and stops. Is it genuinely a goal to leave this open to including new entity types, such that those groups are aggregates of multiple types of other entities? This seems likely to cause more confusion about ID namespaces and collisions. If they will affect naming and key constraints, it seems better to articulate and document these anticipated expansions up front. 

Even if encompassing other entity types is a goal, does it make sense to do so by employing a broader term (`locations`) which is not only an entity type defined in the same extension, but also not currently allowed in the groups, and also one of the subtypes you might want to encompass in the future? That is to say: We've got a type called `S` and a type called `L`. We've got another type that is currently a `Set of S`, but might someday expand to be a `Set of (S or L or ...)`. The proposal is to handle this eventuality by giving `Set of S` the name `Set of L`. This seems really confusing, and my impression is that it can only be for historical reasons, not because it is consistent or helps people understand the spec or resulting data.

> 2. I don't think "location" is inaccurate for a file that only references stops either; in the spec, stops are called "locations" and even have associated `location_types`.

I agree, the term is not inaccurate. But the term is very broad and could apply to a large number of things both in and out of the flex routing domain (most notably the entities in the table `locations.txt`). Someone reading the GTFS spec or working with a GTFS feed may be approaching it for the first time, or may not need to use flex services at all. They should be able to readily and intuitively identify which entities serve which purposes and relate to one another. "Location Groups" does give an indication that these are groups of other entities, but not that those other entities are stops, and that the whole construct is only used in a particular extension called "flex" for on-demand transit. A name like "flex_stop_groups" clearly signals all these things. Again, I am not insisting on any particular term like "flex". The core idea is that entities could be clearly and consistently named, and ideally grouped by extension or purpose.

Perhaps the most important point here: this extension defines an entity called `location`s, and these `location_group`s are *not groups of `locations`*. This is inconsistent and is almost certain to be confusing or frustrating for people to work with. It seems questionable to bake such inconsistencies into a specification before it's even adopted.

> 3. In my opinion, including the word "stop" in the file name causes more confusion considering there are more instances of that word elsewhere in the spec: `stop_areas.txt`, `stop_times.txt`, `stops.txt`, not to mention all the field names with the word "stop." `stop_areas.txt` is an especially important case because it actually has the same relational function as location_groups, only for a different component of the spec (fares). Imagine having two files named `stop_areas.txt` and `stop_groups.txt` that are **nearly functionally identical**, but meant for different purposes.

I don't understand how it causes confusion to include the word "stop" in the name of an entity that is a group of stops. The word "stop" appears in many places because stops are fundamental entities in GTFS, and many other entities are related to them. Any chosen term also becomes less confusing if it's qualified to give context (which component, extension, aggregate it belongs to) e.g. `flex_stop_groups`.

The kind of confusion you're referring to here is too many entities including a particular word, which follows from the structure of the data and could be addressed by hierarchy or grouping. The kind of confusion I'm referring to is terms and their combinations contradicting the structure of the data. The latter concerns me more.

> In our last working group meeting, it was decided to move the table defining stop groups from being shared with fares v2 in `stop_areas.txt` back to using a dedicated file `location_groups.txt`.

This could be justified just on the basis of them being different optional, self-contained spec extensions. Again I'm thinking about gtfs-components here. The way GTFS and its spec are broken into modules or components would need to be finalized before it would be clear if this is sufficient reason to have separate tables.

> `stop_areas.txt` has a companion, `areas.txt`. `stop_areas` only assign stops to areas, and multiple entries in `stop_areas` can have the same `area_id`, without including any attributes. The `area_id` in `areas.txt` is a unique ID, and areas.txt contains attributes like `area_name`. When other tables reference the `area_id`, they reference `areas.area_id` rather than `stop_areas.area_id`.

Something like `areas.txt` you are describing here is what I meant in my other comments by "materializing" the implicit location_groups in a table. This seems like a normalized relational model. As such it will be readily approachable and easier to grasp for many people. Arguably, it's not just "easier", but it only becomes possible to validate and reason about clearly when it adheres to certain principles. 

Just to be sure: the values appearing in `areas.area_id` and those in `stop_areas.area_id` are drawn from exactly the same set of values right? The set is just defined by the unique values in `areas`, then those same values are referenced in `stop_areas`? In standard terminology, they are the primary keys of `areas` and foreign keys in `stop_areas`? If so yes, this makes sense to me (though I find the naming of the tables a bit odd, something like `area_stops` seems more conventional).

This fare-oriented area-of-stops structure does seem very similar to the one that would be needed in flex routing though, so it is certainly worth asking if you need/want separate tables for the two. Strict componentization of GTFS seems like the main justification. If the attributes of areas/zones/groups are expected to remain identical for the fare and flex use cases, they can just share the tables. If the cases are (even potentially) divergent enough they can have different tables, at the cost of making the spec more complex but more modular.

> However, the current `location_groups.txt` combines both "grouping" and "indicating attributes" within a single table.

Right, it seems like a denormalized form of the fare-oriented area-of-stops.

> What if we introduce a file similar to `areas.txt` for `location_groups.txt`? 

This would not only be more consistent with other parts of GTFS (other "gtfs-components" you could say), it would be more consistent with decades of practice and theory underpinning databases and data modeling. Not necessarily introduce a file, but at least introduce the abstract entity (see below).

> * **Perhaps alleviate concerns raised in [this comment](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/388#discussion_r1416728745)? (Because the IDs in the new file would be unique ID.)**

Yes, I meant that the wording is probably confusing because the data model does not enable it to be clear. Changing some words in the description wouldn't change the structure they're trying to describe. Introducing distinct types/tables and normalizing the data (i.e. factoring redundant data or implicit entities out into their own tables) might allow for wording that is less confusing to the reader because it is able to refer more closely to the structure of the data in the files people see in front of them. On the other hand, if there aren't any redundant attributes to be factored out into this new table (in this case, the flex equivalent of fare-oriented areas) other than the IDs, you could elect to not materialize it. But in that case the entity *still exists in the model*, and should still be described in the documentation, it is just elided from the physical tables in the feed for convenience of feed producers (though It's debatable how convenient that is if they already have the table in their software). To be specific, you can say "There is this entity called a location_group, and each one has an ID that is unique among all location_groups, stops, and locations. However, these entities have no properties of their own, so they currently don't need a table. They're implicitly instantiated by reference from foreign keys in location_groups.txt." or to drop the jargon, "created when someone references their ID in this other table". 

Of course I still think renaming these things makes sense. The table location_groups would more rightly be the flex equivalent of your fare-oriented areas, and a table called something like location_group_stops would then associate stops to location_groups. In my opinion this all gets much less confusing if the tables are called flex_zones and flex_zone_stops. And even less confusing if you also have consistent naming with fare_areas and fare_area_stops.

I want to emphasize that I'm not making this stuff up as I go along or asking people to adopt "my way". I am just trying to describe standard data modeling and database design as practiced and refined for the last 50 years and taught in every computer science curriculum. It's founded in mathematics and decades of reasoning, not my personal opinion. Anything I say here may be flawed, and should be confronted with this standard practice and theory.

People with any background in data modeling or databases are already performing this mental transform into clear, standard language every time they read the spec. It's not so bad to convert the language, but it can get really frustrating when the underlying structure is too idiosyncratic or ad-hoc.

body:
> This wording was recently changed to be clearer than it was before. Suggestions to further improve the wording would definitely be welcome!

To summarize a previous comment, it will be straightforward to make the wording clearer if the data model it's describing is clearer. It may also be impossible to verify that the system of entities and relationships is consistent if they are not modeled using the right tools and concepts.

> From a producer perspective, it is more laborious to have to maintain single location groups using **two** files.

As someone who regularly creates small GTFS feeds by hand in a text editor (for software test cases) I get this. It's nice that GTFS is human-writable. On the other hand it's not particularly hard to make two short text files instead of one, and I am not sure hand-editing is common. There's just a trade-off in convenience (which I've addressed in other comments) that requires a design decision. In my view, if a decision is made to elide tables when those tables would contain only IDs, the entity types themselves should still be described in the documentation or data model. And this decision should ideally be consistent across base GTFS and all GTFS extensions: fares, flex, and whatever other extensions should consistently elide tables in the same way, in a manner that is clearly explained to the reader as a general rule.

If GTFS or certain extensions to GTFS are intended to be primarily machine-readable, and especially machine-*writable*, the second table is a non-issue. Software that is able to internally represent areas made up of stops, then write them out to GTFS can trivially produce the two tables instead of one. The real question here seems to be whether GTFS-flex is designed to be hand-writable.

> I'll have to take your word that this feature deviates from conventional structuring of data, but Flex as a spec itself deviates from convention, to use @leonardehrenfried's words, these considerations are the easy part of implementing Flex.

You don't need to take my word for it, and I'm truly not asking you to. Data modeling is a very standardized and well-documented discipline, and there are many excellent books and articles about it. People much more skilled and specialized than us have spent countless years perfecting the thinking behind it, and observing what works and what fails while applying it to intricate, mission-critical systems. All we have to do is read their conclusions and best practices, and choose which ones to follow. If we want people to understand and use what we create, and most importantly if we want to be able to reason about whether it's correct or consistent, we do need to pay attention to that body of work.

I'm not sure what you mean by "these considerations are the easy part". Do you mean consuming unusually structured data will be relatively easy, compared to actually doing something with the data? That could be true - it may just require each consumer to create their own model and reimplement some similar conversion or normalization logic (though it's still not clear why we'd want to force everyone to do that instead of just thinking carefully about the specification). But this assumes the "unconventional" data is fundamentally meaningful and consistent, and just needs a little conversion. "Conventional" may be the wrong word here: I'm not talking about just doing things most other people do (although that's useful for comprehension), I'm talking about following conventions that were adopted *because they enable correct reasoning and representation*.

> We really could spend an endless amount of time iterating components of the spec like this, but at the end of the day, consumers will still need to contend with the bigger challenge of implementing flexible routing. 

I think both deserve attention, and over time there will likely be far more producers and consumers than people working on the spec, so it may be far more efficient to invest effort at the specification stage.

> But I still wonder if the two file approach is less complex for a consumer and if mitigating that complexity outweighs the increased complexity for producers? 

If both ends are software systems, rather than people editing a text file by hand, there is no appreciable difference in complexity. Both ends will in one form or another have a representation of both the groups and the entities that make them up. They will have a type T and an instance of a collection or container holding T. In most cases using GTFS will just look like a round-trip through object-relational mapping.

> To my knowledge, no Flex consumer since Flex v2's publication over three years ago has ever raised this as an inherent issue of location groups. Yes, areas/stop_areas.txt was momentarily used instead, but for the sole reason of reducing redundancy of file functionality, not because it used two files.

It's not that they couldn't make it work. It might be possible to handle each new extension as an ad-hoc one-off approach that each new group of people needs to learn and understand separately. If you're lucky it won't contain any critical inconsistencies that come back and bite you, or the thousands of people using it 10 years from now.

But other people have already done all the hard work figuring out how to describe and reason about these topics since the 1970s. I find it really odd to revert to how things were done before I was born, and condemn ourselves to repeatedly speed-running 50 years of frustration and bugs. It's very helpful to just "read the manual" and use shared language and tools.

I'm also not arguing for making GTFS super-complicated Netex style. GTFS succeeded due to pragmatism - I get that and I like it. But let's avoid extremes. If you look at the original core GTFS spec it's immediately recognizable as a relational model. That's because it's dump of a relational database. It has benefitted from that underlying structure. If subsequent extensions do not mesh well with that existing basis and share its terminology and concepts, the specification will become increasingly incoherent and hard to understand.

To that I would add:
- Rather than just prefixing extension names, consider completely renaming entities to narrow meaning and resolve contradictions (e.g. location_groups are not made of locations) (this may already be implied in your point 2)
- Extend table naming scheme uniformly to other proposals and tables, e.g.: `extension_entity[_subentity]`
- Consider introducing additional entities or "supertypes" to the specification that coherently capture why different tables share an ID namespace. e.g. flex routes reference a stop-like entity class that encompass normal stops, but also a couple of other things. These conceptual supertypes do not need to be materialized in tables, but their existence in the specification and description could make it much easier to understand.

Note that I will probably not be able to attend any meetings on this topic. But please feel free to take my commentary into consideration when working on next steps at any planned meeting.  

I think more so than written vs. spoken communication, there are other aspects of the change proposal and adoption process that impede clear understanding and discussion. But I hope to raise those points on a new issue or #413, not on this pre-existing proposal.

Are the Stop FeedEntities required to be ordered before the TripModifications when combined in one feed? If not, is the consumer then required to filter, buffer, and reorder the messages it receives to ensure referential integrity (that new stops are known and created before being referenced by TripModifications?) How would this work in streaming differential cases?

The fact that the comment uses both the terms "stops" and "stop times", which already have defined meanings in GTFS, to refer to the same thing (a field and message type called `replacement_stops`) is confusing, requiring the reader to dig into the ReplacementStop message and discover that it provides information allowing the consumer to synthesize new stop times by adding delays to existing scheduled stop_times, referencing existing or newly created stops. I'd recommend revising terminology for consistency - readers will perceive terms to mean what they've been defined to mean within GTFS. Or at least rephrase the comment to explain more clearly.

+# Trip Modifications
+
+A `TripModifications` message identifies a list of similar `trip_ids` from the (CSV) GTFS sharing the same stop pattern, which are all affected by particular modifications, such as a detour.
+
+## SLO: Service-level objective
+
+The frequency of data updates is expected to be approximately hourly (~24 times/day). Ingestion time may depend on the total number of affected trips. Consumers are expected to ingest a single TripModification within 5 minutes, and a feed with hundreds of detours within 20 minutes.
+
+## TripModifications
+
+The `TripModifications` is in effect on all of the listed service\_dates, until it is removed from the feed. On any given service date, a trip MUST NOT be assigned to more than one `TripModifications` object.
+
+There MAY be multiple `TripModifications` for a given stop pattern. It may be desirable to split the trips into multiple modifications e.g. if the `propagated_modification_delay` changes significantly, over the course of the detour.
+
+The trips created through GTFS-TripModifications modify and replace each specified `trip_id`, and don't create a copy or additional run. Modifications are applied on the schedule information, like if a static GTFS (CSV) was modified. 
+
+The scheduled stop times of each replacement trip are created from those of the affected trip, by performing the changes listed in modifications. `stop_sequence` for all stop times are replaced by a new value of 1 to n, starting with 1 on the first stop_time and increasing by 1 for each stop in the trip. A `TripUpdate` message must be provided to publish real-time arrival/departure times for the replacement trip.
+
+
+## Linkage to TripUpdates
+
+* A TripUpdate SHOULD be provided using a `ModifiedTripSelector` inside the TripUpdate's `TripDescriptor`. 
+    * When the TripUpdate refers to the replacement trip, the consumer should behave as if the static GTFS would have been modified with the TripModifications (e.g. `arrival_time`, `departure_time`, `stop_sequence`, `stop_id` on replacement stops)
+    * When providing a `ModifiedTripSelector`, the other fields of the `ScheduleRelationship` SHOULD be left empty, to avoid confusion by consumer that aren't looking for the `ModifiedTripSelector` value.

+

+
+The trips created through GTFS-TripModifications modify and replace each specified `trip_id`, and don't create a copy or additional run. Modifications are applied on the schedule information, like if a static GTFS (CSV) was modified. 
+

A `TripUpdate` message must be provided to publish real-time arrival/departure times for the replacement trip.

+
+* A TripUpdate SHOULD be provided using a `ModifiedTripSelector` inside the TripUpdate's `TripDescriptor`. 
+    * When the TripUpdate refers to the replacement trip, the consumer should behave as if the static GTFS would have been modified with the TripModifications (e.g. `arrival_time`, `departure_time`, `stop_sequence`, `stop_id` on replacement stops)
+    * When providing a `ModifiedTripSelector`, the other fields of the `ScheduleRelationship` SHOULD be left empty, to avoid confusion by consumer that aren't looking for the `ModifiedTripSelector` value. 
+    * Providing a TripUpdate with the a `ModifiedTripSelector` is the only way to create predictions at replacement stops
+* If no such TripUpdate is found, TripUpdates for the original `trip_id` will apply to the modified trip. 
+    * In this case, the static GTFS information used should be from the static GTFS before any TripModifications applied. 
+    * Real time can be available to the common stops between the previous trip and the new modified trip, no ETA is available at the replacement stops.
+
+##  Modification
+
+A `Modification` message replaces a span of n stop times (`num_stops_replaced`) from each affected trip starting at `start_stop_sequence`. The spans of the modifications MUST not overlap. Spans may not be contiguous; in this case the two modifications MUST be merged into one.  These stop times are replaced with a new stop time for each replacement stop described by `replacement_stops`.
+
+The sequence of `replacement_stops` may be of arbitrary length. For example, 3 stops could be replaced by 2, 4, or 0 stops as the situation may require.
+
+![](images/trip_modification.png)
+
+_An example showing the effect of a modification on a particular trip. This modification may also be applied to several other trips._
+
+![](images/propagated_delay.png)
+
+_Propagated detour delays affect all stops following the end of a modification. If a trip has multiple modifications, the delays are accumulated._
+

+
+Each `ReplacementStop` message defines a stop that will now be visited by the trip, and optionally specifies the estimated travel time to the stop. The `ReplacementStop` message is used to construct the scheduled `stop_time` for the stop.

+When `travel_time_to_stop` is specified, the `arrival_time` is calculated from a reference stop in the original trip, plus the offset in `travel_time_to_stop`. Otherwise, the `arrival_time` can be be interpolated based on the total duration of the modification in the original trip.

+The `departure_time` always equals the `arrival_time`.

+# Trip Modifications
+
+A `TripModifications` message identifies a list of similar `trip_ids` from the (CSV) GTFS sharing the same stop pattern, which are all affected by particular modifications, such as a detour.
+
+## SLO: Service-level objective
+
+The frequency of data updates is expected to be approximately hourly (~24 times/day). Ingestion time may depend on the total number of affected trips. Consumers are expected to ingest a single TripModification within 5 minutes, and a feed with hundreds of detours within 20 minutes.
+
+## TripModifications
+
+The `TripModifications` is in effect on all of the listed service\_dates, until it is removed from the feed. On any given service date, a trip MUST NOT be assigned to more than one `TripModifications` object.
+
+There MAY be multiple `TripModifications` for a given stop pattern. It may be desirable to split the trips into multiple modifications e.g. if the `propagated_modification_delay` changes significantly, over the course of the detour.
+
+The trips created through GTFS-TripModifications modify and replace each specified `trip_id`, and don't create a copy or additional run. Modifications are applied on the schedule information, like if a static GTFS (CSV) was modified. 
+
+The scheduled stop times of each replacement trip are created from those of the affected trip, by performing the changes listed in modifications. `stop_sequence` for all stop times are replaced by a new value of 1 to n, starting with 1 on the first stop_time and increasing by 1 for each stop in the trip. A `TripUpdate` message must be provided to publish real-time arrival/departure times for the replacement trip.
+
+
+## Linkage to TripUpdates
+
+* A TripUpdate SHOULD be provided using a `ModifiedTripSelector` inside the TripUpdate's `TripDescriptor`. 
+    * When the TripUpdate refers to the replacement trip, the consumer should behave as if the static GTFS would have been modified with the TripModifications (e.g. `arrival_time`, `departure_time`, `stop_sequence`, `stop_id` on replacement stops)
+    * When providing a `ModifiedTripSelector`, the other fields of the `ScheduleRelationship` SHOULD be left empty, to avoid confusion by consumer that aren't looking for the `ModifiedTripSelector` value.

body: Issue created - https://github.com/google/transit/issues/392

The Stop is situated in a separate FeedEntity, outside the TripModification. Each FeedEntity contains exactly one sub-entity. In a message-oriented system transmitting individual differential updates, each containing one or more FeedEntities, how long should the receiver wait after receiving a TripModification that references a stop before it applies that update? When is the "safe" point to stop buffering and resolve the buffered/accumulated messages with respect to one another? If it receives a Stop message which alters an existing stop after it receives the TripModification, which version of the Stop does that TripModification reference? How will the receiver know whether a TripUpdate it has just received is intended to reference a stop that will be sent in a later message? How long is the sender allowed to wait before it supplies the Stops that the receiver is waiting for? At what point is it an error not to send Stops you've referenced? There are many questions like this that can likely be covered by a set of simple rules, but those rules would still need to be specified. 

One such rule is that messages may only reference entities created or modified in other messages that were sent before them. Another possible rule is that sending a message that updates an existing entity means all previously sent messages referencing that entity now reference the revised version of the entity (though this rule is not sufficient on its own to define what happens when the stop is not pre-existing).

https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/dos-donts/#add-required
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18196288

Generally speaking, new "required" fields in protobufs are discouraged.  It's less about high-level goals of data validation and more about what happens when different data producers and consumers (and intermediates) with slightly different specs are involved + nuances of the protobuf implementation itself.

I actually thought about flagging this originally, since I was trying to think of a case where we might not specify a `stop_id` as part of `Stop` at some point down the road (maybe it's possible?).  But I would not add more required fields unnecessarily.

Is the “can be” in your reply meant exactly as “can be” or would you view that more as “should be” or “must be”? And does the can/should/must change depending on how far in advance of the start time of the trip the agency/producer determines a trip will start late?

My concern is that without more explicit guidance on when to use REPLACEMENT there will be producers using it in different ways. And this most recent set of questions is intended as a thought exercise to point out some of the ambiguity that I think needs to be cleared up.

Here is a first effort at adding more guidance on when to use and not use REPLACEMENT. I’m not sure it removes all ambiguity but thought I’d share it for feedback:

REPLACEMENT can be (this “can be” is intended to convey it’s optional and a producer could use SCHEDULED and other fields in the specification instead) used when a trip follows a different stop pattern than scheduled in the GTFS or when a trip follows its usual stop pattern but with different scheduled stop times that the agency communicates to customers as new scheduled times. REPLACEMENT must not be used to communicate real-time schedule deviations (predictions) as SCHEUDLED should be used in this case.

+## Migration Guide - Transition from ADDED to NEW or DUPLICATED trips

+The GTFS-realtime `trip.schedule_relationship` of `NEW` represents a new trip that runs on a schedule unrelated to any existing scheduled trip.

+This migration guide defines how existing producers and consumers that were using the `ADDED` enumeration should transition to either the `NEW` and the `DUPLICATED` enumeration. The goal is to minimize disruption to producers and consumers during the transition. 
+
+*If you are a producer or consumer that has **not** used the `ADDED` enumeration, no action is required - you can produce/consume `NEW` and/or `DUPLICATED` trips without producing/consuming any `ADDED` entities.*

+For a full history of the `NEW` enumeration, see the [`NEW` and `REPLACEMENT` proposal on GitHub](https://github.com/google/transit/pull/504).

+### Which one to migrate to
+
+Both `NEW` and `DUPLICATED` enumeration are used to specify a trip which was not originally scheduled to run in the GTFS static.
+
+Use `NEW` if your trip cannot be described using any scheduled trips as a template. For example, if the trip calls at different stops from the regular trips of the route, or if the extra trip is pickup only at the beginning of the route despite that the regular trips allow both pickup and drop off at all stops.
+

+### Using ADDED and NEW entities in the same feed
+
+If you are a producer who has been using the `ADDED` enumeration to specify trips which are unrelated to the schedule, to avoid disruption to existing consumers it is recommended that you continue to produce `ADDED` entitles for these trips but also add `NEW` entitles for the same trip.

body:
I'm sorry, but as Google mentioned, we can't break backward compatibility.

A decade ago, when REPLACEMENT was removed from the spec, there was a version of .proto file without that value published, and it horribly broke consumers on existing feeds when they were compiled with an updated .proto . Therefore the value has been put back and marked as deprecated.

Therefore the value ADDED has to remain even if we don't want to use it anymore, and those consumers who are using ADDED for the purpose I am migrating to NEW (like OpenTripPlanner) can treat it the same as NEW instead.

Let me be up front that if we are considering a version bump to GTFS-Realtime (either major or minor), then I don't think we'd do it for just this proposal.  We've never done a version bump of GTFS-Realtime, so this would need a broader discussion of whether we'd actually do it, what the process looks like, expectations around support for old and new versions, and if we come to terms with all that, then an extended phase where we discuss any other breaking-changes that we'd want to roll into the new version (think something akin to the GBFS process).

Which is to say, I don't want you to be surprised if/when I vote -1 on any single proposal here with a version bump.

+# Guiding principles
+
+In order to preserve the original vision of GTFS, a number of guiding principles have been established to take into consideration when changing the specification:
+
+**Feeds should be easy to create and edit**  
+We chose CSV as the basis for the specification because it's easy to view and edit using spreadsheet programs and text editors, which is helpful for smaller agencies. It's also straightforward to generate from most programming languages and databases, which is good for publishers of larger feeds.
+
+**Feeds should be easy to parse**  
+Feed readers should be able to extract the information they're looking for with as little work as possible. Changes and additions to the feed should be as broadly useful as possible, to minimize the number of code paths that readers of the feed need to implement. (However, making creation easier should be given precedence, since there will ultimately be more feed publishers than feed readers.)

I don't think one follows from the other. Parentheses could be removed from the final sentence as it's as important as any other information here.

+# Guiding principles
+
+In order to preserve the original vision of GTFS, a number of guiding principles have been established to take into consideration when changing the specification:
+
+**Feeds should be easy to create and edit**  
+We chose CSV as the basis for the specification because it's easy to view and edit using spreadsheet programs and text editors, which is helpful for smaller agencies. It's also straightforward to generate from most programming languages and databases, which is good for publishers of larger feeds.
+
+**Feeds should be easy to parse**  
+Feed readers should be able to extract the information they're looking for with as little work as possible. Changes and additions to the feed should be as broadly useful as possible, to minimize the number of code paths that readers of the feed need to implement. (However, making creation easier should be given precedence, since there will ultimately be more feed publishers than feed readers.)
+
+**The spec is about passenger information**  
+GTFS is primarily concerned with passenger information. That is, the spec should include information that can help power tools for riders, first and foremost. There is potentially a large amount of operations-oriented information that transit agencies might want to transmit internally between systems. +# Introduction to GTFS Governance
+
+The GTFS standard is not set in stone; it is an open specification developed and maintained by a community of transit agencies, developers, and other stakeholders who actively use it. As this community of GTFS data producers and consumers continues to evolve, proposals for extending the specification to support new capabilities are expected. To manage this process, a GTFS governance framework has been established.
+
+GTFS governance refers to the framework that guides how the GTFS is maintained, updated, and developed. It encompasses the rules and processes that the community has established to guide decision-making, ensuring that GTFS remains an open and collaborative data standard.

+
+* [Guiding principles](guiding-principles.md)  
+* [Roles and responsibilities](roles.md)  
+* [Change types](change-types.md)
+* [Change process](change-process.md)

+
+The community is composed of two main stakeholder categories: [Contributors](#contributors) and the [Maintainer](#maintainer).

+

+
+A GTFS Producer is an individual or organization responsible for generating GTFS data. This may include transit agencies, data vendors, aggregators, or planners.
+
+* If an individual or organization assigns GTFS feed production to another party, only one of them can be recognized as the Producer.  
+* To vote, Producers must reference the GTFS feed they represent to confirm their role as Producer.  
+* In the case where a contributor is both a Consumer and Producer, they can only count as one, thus they must select a single role to represent during testing and voting.
+
+#### Consumers
+
+A GTFS Consumer is an individual or organization that ingests GTFS data, typically to provide and distribute rider-facing transit information through platforms such as software applications.
+
+* In some cases, contributors may consume GTFS data for research, data analysis, operations, planning, etc. However, they are considered Consumers only if their work is publicly accessible or shared in a public-facing context.  
+* To vote, consumers must reference the GTFS consuming application they represent to confirm their role as Consumer.  
+* In the case where a contributor is both a Consumer and Producer, they can only count as one, thus they must select a single role to represent during testing and voting.
+

+# Guiding principles
+
+In order to preserve the original vision of GTFS, a number of guiding principles have been established to take into consideration when changing the specification:
+
+**Feeds should be easy to create and edit**  
+We chose CSV as the basis for the specification because it's easy to view and edit using spreadsheet programs and text editors, which is helpful for smaller agencies. It's also straightforward to generate from most programming languages and databases, which is good for publishers of larger feeds.
+
+**Feeds should be easy to parse**  
+Feed readers should be able to extract the information they're looking for with as little work as possible. Changes and additions to the feed should be as broadly useful as possible, to minimize the number of code paths that readers of the feed need to implement. (However, making creation easier should be given precedence, since there will ultimately be more feed publishers than feed readers.)

We would like to wait until this proposal is finalized before initiating that conversation with the community. In the meantime, we will add it as an item in the governance backlog.

+
+In order to preserve the original vision of GTFS, a number of guiding principles have been established to take into consideration when changing the specification:
+
+**Feeds should be easy to create and edit**  
+We chose CSV as the basis for the specification because it's easy to view and edit using spreadsheet programs and text editors, which is helpful for smaller agencies. It's also straightforward to generate from most programming languages and databases, which is good for publishers of larger feeds.
